title: Can Creatine Help With Depression?
hook: Best known for building muscle, creatine is now being tested against depression — a review of five trials found real benefit in some studies of women, but no effect in others.
key_points: Creatine may help treat depression by boosting the brain's energy supply, not just muscle.
A review pooled five randomized clinical trials with 238 participants total.
Two trials — both in women with major depressive disorder — found adding creatine to standard treatment improved symptoms.
Three other trials found no meaningful benefit, so the evidence overall is mixed.
content_html: Creatine has a well-earned reputation as a muscle-building supplement. Now researchers are testing whether it might help with something very different: depression.
extra_html:
As ScienceDaily reports, the theory rests on creatine's role in cellular energy — the same mechanism that helps muscles work harder may also support brain cells that struggle with energy supply in depression. A review examined five randomized clinical trials covering 238 participants and found a mixed picture. Two trials, both involving women with major depressive disorder, reported that adding creatine to standard treatment improved symptoms. Three other trials found no meaningful benefit.

The honest read here is "promising but unproven." The positive results are concentrated in a specific group — women with major depressive disorder — and the overall trial base is still small. It's not yet the kind of evidence that supports adding creatine to a depression treatment plan, but it's enough to justify larger, more targeted trials to see whether the early signal holds up.

related.hook: Depression and anxiety are among the most common — and most treatable — health conditions. Knowing the signs is the first step to getting help that works.

flashcards.prompt: What's the theory behind using creatine as a depression treatment?
flashcards.back_html: Creatine is best known for building muscle, but it also helps supply energy to cells — including brain cells. The theory is that boosting the brain's energy supply could help ease depression symptoms.
